_meta.purpose: Whole-page templates the picker chooses from a 4.0 brief (engine.page_sequence.select_for_brief) by its structured fields only: page_sequence, then stage, then page, then product_type refined by platforms, primary_side and primary_action, then primary_action or platforms alone, then project_type mobile-app, and general-landing when none says what the page is, with why naming the field to set. No industry and no word of the brief's prose picks a sequence. picked_by says which fields reach each entry. A section with a proof kind renders only with the client's real proof of that kind. mechanism_needs names what each conversion mechanism needs (a proof kind or a contact route); without_phone is a section's text when the client has no phone; with_phone_sign_in is its text when the product signs users in by phone (sign_in). job names what each section does for the ask: ask, proof, objection, explanation or navigation; explains_category marks a section that argues for the category, which a visitor who arrives by the brand's name does not need.

entries.picked_by: product_type local-service, or primary_action quote, book or contact

section_sequence.purpose: Capture the lead at first paint. Text left (headline + one-line value + phone affordance), inline quote or contact form right. The form is the wow moment and the conversion path, never buried below.
section_sequence.without_phone: Capture the lead at first paint. Text left (headline + one-line value), inline quote or contact form right. The form is the wow moment and the conversion path, never buried below.

section_sequence.purpose: A thin band of 3-5 real, organic numbers (jobs completed, years operating, response time, coverage radius) directly under the hero: instant credibility before the scroll.
3-5 cards naming the concrete reasons to choose this service (speed, price transparency, licensing, same-day). Each card has a tight heading and one sentence.
Every service category / sector the business covers, rendered as a scannable row of pills. Map EVERY sector from the source into a pill. Do not trim to a tidy few.
Every concrete offering (every skip size, every package, every product line) as its own card with a spec line and an action. Completeness over neatness: one source item -> one card.
2-column zig-zag rows that expand the marquee differentiators with depth: alternating media/text, each row earning its own visual. Not a 3-equal-card grid.
Where the service operates: a map, a region list, or a coverage statement. For a local/commercial service this answers the 'do you cover me?' question that gates the lead.
A named, quantified testimonial or a strong pull-quote with attribution (name, role/company). One strong quote beats fifteen vibes-only blurbs.
A focused conversion band repeating the primary action (get a quote / call now) with the phone affordance, after the page has earned the click.
section_sequence.without_phone: A focused conversion band repeating the primary action (get a quote), after the page has earned the click.

section_sequence.purpose: A sitemap footer: services, coverage areas, company, contact (phone + hours), legal. Generosity after the page's restraint, never a thin one-row strip.
section_sequence.without_phone: A sitemap footer: services, coverage areas, company, contact (the routes the client offers, and hours), legal. Generosity after the page's restraint, never a thin one-row strip.

entries.cta_placement: Primary lead-capture in the hero (inline form) and repeated in a dedicated CTA band before the footer; phone number persistent in header and CTA band.
entries.footer: Rich sitemap footer: Services, Coverage areas, Company, Contact (phone + hours), Legal.
entries.notes: The inline hero form is the conversion path. Proof and the phone come from the client: a proof section renders only with the client's real numbers or named quotes, and the phone affordance only with a real number; without them the picker drops them and says why. Map every sector into a pill, every size or package into an item card, every benefit into a value card. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.
entries.cta_placement_without_phone: Primary lead-capture in the hero (inline form) and repeated in a dedicated CTA band before the footer.
entries.footer_without_phone: Rich sitemap footer: Services, Coverage areas, Company, Contact (routes + hours), Legal.

section_sequence.purpose: Asymmetric hero: value headline + one-line lede + primary CTA on one side, a real product mock (screenshot or interactive demo) on the other. The mock is the proof.
A single monochrome customer-logo row near the hero: social proof before the feature tour. Skip if there are no real logos.
3-5 outcome-led cards (not feature lists), each with a concrete claim with a number where possible.
3-5 marquee feature sections, each a 2-column zig-zag with a deep visual (annotated screenshot, before/after, synthetic UI). Depth over a dense feature grid.
The integrations or ecosystem the product plugs into, as a labelled grid of marks. Maps EVERY integration the source lists.
A stats band of real outcomes (latency, time saved, adoption), organic numbers, not round marketing figures.
A named, quantified customer quote or mini case study with attribution and a real metric.
A 'starts at $X' teaser linking out to full pricing, never a full pricing table on the homepage.
A focused sign-up / start-free band repeating the single primary action.
Sitemap footer by audience: Product, Solutions, Resources, Company, Legal.

entries.cta_placement: Single primary CTA (start free / sign up) in the hero, repeated in the CTA band; secondary 'see the demo' allowed once in the hero.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer by audience: Product, Solutions, Resources, Company, Legal.
entries.notes: One primary path. Map every integration into the integrations grid and every differentiator into its own split feature row. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

section_sequence.purpose: Product imagery gallery on one side, buy box (title, price, variant pickers, add-to-cart) on the other. The buy box is the conversion path, above the fold.
A thin band of trust signals: free shipping threshold, returns window, secure checkout, in-stock status.
Cards covering the concrete reasons to buy (materials, warranty, what's in the box) and a spec line.
Every variant, size, or option as a selectable card/swatch. Map EVERY option the source lists: one variant, one tile.
Zig-zag rows telling the product story with real photography or detail shots: craft, use, results.
Real, attributed reviews with a rating distribution: named, specific, not 'amazing!'.
A small, curated set of related products, not an endless grid.

The objection-handling section: shipping, returns, sizing, care. Answers the questions that block checkout. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
A sticky or repeated add-to-cart band so the conversion action is always reachable.
Sitemap footer: Shop, Help (shipping/returns), Company, Legal, contact.

entries.cta_placement: Add-to-cart in the buy box above the fold, made persistent via a sticky bar and repeated in a CTA band.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: Shop, Help (shipping & returns), Company, Legal, contact.
entries.notes: Conversion is the buy box. Vary image aspect ratios; never clip every shot to 1:1. Map every variant into the option grid; every spec into a card. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

section_sequence.purpose: A confident positioning statement with a peek of selected work. Editorial, asymmetric: the work carries the page.
An irregular, editorial grid of case studies (varied aspect ratios, generous gaps). Each tile is a real project, not a card box.
What the studio does, as capability cards or a list. Map EVERY discipline the source lists.
1-3 deep case studies as zig-zag rows: problem, approach, result with a real metric.
How the studio works: a few honest steps, not numbered chapter signposting for its own sake.
A monochrome client-logo wall or named testimonials with attribution.
Who's behind the work: real people, real photos or styled portraits.
A direct 'start a project / let's talk' band with a real contact path.
Sitemap footer: Work, Services, About, Contact, social.

entries.cta_placement: Primary 'start a project / get in touch' in the hero secondary slot and repeated in a dedicated CTA band; contact details in the footer.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: Work, Services, About, Contact, social.
entries.notes: The work is the proof; description is supplementary. Use varied image ratios and an irregular grid, never a tidy 3-equal-card row. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

section_sequence.purpose: A masthead with the lead story given editorial weight: big headline, real image, byline. Sets the publication's voice.
An editorial grid of featured pieces with varied prominence (one dominant, several secondary), not equal cards.
Every section/topic the publication covers, as a row of pills. Map EVERY category from the source.
A scannable list of recent pieces with byline, date, and reading time, typographic, not boxed.
A highlighted piece or a pull-quote that carries the editorial point of view, with attribution.
An inline newsletter capture (not a timed modal) with a clear value line and a single email field.
Who writes here: real contributors with names and roles.
A focused subscribe band repeating the newsletter or membership action.
Sitemap footer: Sections, Archive, About, Subscribe, legal.

entries.cta_placement: Inline newsletter / subscribe capture mid-page and repeated in a CTA band; never a first-paint modal.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: Sections, Archive, About, Subscribe, legal.
entries.notes: Typography and hierarchy carry the page. Map every topic into a category pill and every recent piece into the list. Newsletter capture is inline, never a timed interstitial. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: product_type app with a store platform (ios or android) in platforms, or project_type mobile-app

section_sequence.purpose: A device mock (real app screen) beside a value headline and app-store badges. The store badges are the conversion path, above the fold.
A thin band of real numbers (downloads, rating, active users), organic, not round marketing figures.
3-5 cards naming what the app does for the user, each with a concrete benefit.
Real app screenshots in device frames showing the key flows: varied, not all clipped to one ratio.
Zig-zag rows expanding the marquee features with a screenshot each, depth over a dense grid.
Named, specific app-store reviews or a rating breakdown, not 'great app!'.
A short, honest set of steps from install to value.
A focused download band repeating the store badges and the single primary action.
Sitemap footer: App, Support, Company, Legal, store links.

entries.cta_placement: App-store badges in the hero and repeated in a download CTA band; rating shown near the badges as a trust signal.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: App, Support, Company, Legal, store links.
entries.notes: Conversion is the store badge. Use real device-framed screenshots with varied crops. Map every feature into a split row and every screen into the gallery. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: product_type marketplace with primary_side demand or unset, or primary_side alone

section_sequence.purpose: Who buys from whom, in one headline, and the primary action: open an account or request access. A real product view (the catalog, an order, the app) on the other side. The supplier path is a secondary link, never a second filled button.
Two panels side by side, one per side of the market, each with what that side gets and its own action. Unequal widths when one side is the main audience.
Every category the catalog carries, as a scannable list or pills. Counts only when the client gives real ones.
Three to five steps from search to delivery: search, compare, order, receive, pay. Real screens where the client has them.
The marquee capabilities (reorder, price comparison, credit, tracking), each a row with a real screen.
Where it delivers, how fast, and the payment terms (credit, cash on delivery, invoices). This answers the questions a trade buyer asks before an account.
Real numbers from the client (buyers, suppliers, orders, cities). Only numbers the client has measured.
One named quote from a real buyer or supplier, with the business name and city.
The real brands or suppliers on the catalog, as one mono row of their marks. The usual trade proof when there are no numbers yet; only marks the client may show.

The objections that stop a trade account: minimum order, delivery windows, returns, credit, who can register. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.

section_sequence.section: CTA band (open an account, or join as a supplier)
section_sequence.purpose: The primary action repeated, with the supplier path as a secondary link.
Sitemap footer: For buyers, For suppliers, Categories, Company, Contact, Legal, app store links when there is an app.

entries.cta_placement: Open an account (or request access) in the hero and the CTA band; the supplier path as a secondary link in both; the app store links in the footer when there is an app.
entries.footer: Rich sitemap footer: For buyers, For suppliers, Categories, Company, Contact, Legal.
entries.notes: A marketplace sells to two sides at once; the page names both and leads with the side the brief names as the main audience. Show the real catalog and ordering screens. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: product_type software with primary_action demo, or primary_action demo alone

section_sequence.purpose: What the product protects or runs, for whom, in one headline; the primary action requests a demo or a call with the team. A real product view or a plain architecture drawing on the other side.
The certificates, audits and regulators the client really holds, each named with its scope. Only ones held; never a badge the client has not earned.
What goes wrong without it, in the buyer's words, with figures only the client has measured.
Three to five steps or a labelled architecture: where it sits, what it touches, what it never sees.
The marquee capabilities, each a row with a real screen or a real output.
The systems it integrates with and the deployment options (cloud, on premises, region), stated plainly.
One mono row of the institutions that use it, only with their permission.
One named quote from a real buyer, with role and institution.

The questions a security or procurement review asks: data residency, access, audits, uptime, contract terms. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
The demo request repeated, with who replies and how fast.
Sitemap footer: Product, Security or trust center, Company, Contact, Legal.

entries.cta_placement: Request a demo in the hero and the CTA band; the nav carries the same action.
entries.footer: Rich sitemap footer: Product, Security, Company, Contact, Legal.
entries.notes: Trust-led: a buyer who must defend the choice to a review board reads the proof first, so the held certifications sit under the hero. Every proof section comes from the client or is dropped. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

section_sequence.purpose: What the product will do and for whom, in one headline. The early-access form is the call to action. The launch status is stated plainly: a date, a season, or in private pilot.
The problem the product solves, in the audience's own words. No figure the client has not measured.
Three to five honest steps, or a real prototype screen labelled as a prototype.
What joining now gives: first access, founding pricing, a say in what gets built. Only what the client will honor.
The real team or founder, named, and why they are building it. Before there are customers, the people are the reason to believe.

When it launches, what it will cost, where it works, what happens to the email address. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
The early-access form repeated, with the launch status.
Contact, legal, social. Short, since there is little to map yet.

entries.cta_placement: The early-access form in the hero and repeated in the CTA band; nothing else asks for the visitor's details.
entries.notes: No proof section before there is proof. A page that shows invented numbers, quotes or client marks spends the trust it is asking for. When a pilot gives real results, move to the live sequence for the business. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: no structured field says what the page is; why names the field to set

section_sequence.purpose: What it is and for whom in one headline, one lede, one primary action, and a real image of the product, the place or the people.
Three to five concrete reasons to choose it, each a heading and one sentence.
Three to five honest steps from first contact to the result.
The two or three things that matter most, each a row with its own real visual.
One named quote from a real customer, with role and company.

The questions that stop the action: price, time, where, what happens next. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
The primary action repeated, after the page has earned it.
Sitemap footer: what it offers, company, contact, legal.

entries.cta_placement: One primary action in the hero, repeated in the CTA band and the nav.
entries.footer: Rich sitemap footer: Offer, Company, Contact, Legal.
entries.notes: The picker's answer when no field or phrase points elsewhere, so a brief always has a skeleton. Set page_sequence when the user names a kind of page. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: page: feature (a page about one feature of a product people already use; stage pre-launch still picks pre-launch)

section_sequence.section: Hero (the feature named + the product's own action)
section_sequence.purpose: Name the feature and what it does for someone who already uses the product, beside a real screen of that feature. The primary action is the one the product really uses for its users (sign in, open the app, or start), never an early-access form: the product has users.
section_sequence.with_phone_sign_in: Name the feature and what it does for someone who already uses the product, beside a real screen of that feature. The primary action is the product's own phone sign-in: one phone number field and a continue button, the code step on the next screen. Never an early-access form: the product has users.

section_sequence.purpose: The task the feature takes over, before and after, in the user's own terms. One idea per screen.
Three to five steps inside the real product, each with the screen it happens on.
The feature's parts, one row each with a real screen. No stock photo stands in for the product.
How the feature connects to the rest of the product, with a link back to the product's home page and to related features.
One named quote from a real user about this feature: name, role, and business or city.

Who has the feature, what it costs, where it works and where it stops. Answers only the questions the client can answer truthfully. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
Repeats the hero's action for a user who has read the page: the same verb, one filled button.
section_sequence.with_phone_sign_in: Repeats the hero's phone sign-in for a user who has read the page: the same phone field and verb, one filled button.

section_sequence.purpose: Sitemap footer: Product (each feature), Support, Company, Legal.

entries.cta_placement: The product's own action in the hero and repeated in the closing band; a link to the product home in the header and in Where it fits.
entries.cta_placement_with_phone_sign_in: The phone sign-in field in the hero and repeated in the closing band; a link to the product home in the header and in Where it fits.
conversion_mechanisms: the product's own action in hero
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: Product (each feature), Support, Company, Legal.
entries.notes: A feature page speaks to people who know the product: no founding team, no early-access form, no launch story. Store badges appear only when the brief's platforms list ios or android. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: platforms without ios or android, where the pick would be the store-app sequence (a product people use in the browser)

section_sequence.purpose: What the product does for its user in one headline, the sign-in or start action the product really uses, and a real screen of the product in the browser. No store badges and no download: it runs on the web.
section_sequence.with_phone_sign_in: What the product does for its user in one headline, then the phone sign-in itself: one phone number field and a continue button, the code step on the next screen. A real screen of the product in the browser beside it. No store badges and no download: it runs on the web.

section_sequence.purpose: The three to five things a user does in the product, each named with its concrete result.
The steps from the first visit to the first result, in the order the product asks for them.
The marquee capabilities, one row each with a real browser screen, depth over a dense grid.
One named quote from a real user: name, and role, business or city.

How sign-in works, what the product keeps about the user, what it costs, which browsers and phones it runs on. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
Repeats the hero's action with the same verb, one filled button.
section_sequence.with_phone_sign_in: Repeats the phone sign-in: the same phone field and verb, one filled button.

section_sequence.purpose: Sitemap footer: Product, Support, Company, Legal.

entries.cta_placement: The sign-in or start action in the hero and the closing band; a sign-in link in the header for returning users.
entries.cta_placement_with_phone_sign_in: The phone sign-in field in the hero and the closing band; a sign-in link in the header for returning users.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: Product, Support, Company, Legal.
entries.notes: The product runs in the browser, so the page has no store badges, no device mock of a store app and no download band. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.

entries.picked_by: primary_side: supply on a two-sided marketplace (the side that lists, sells, delivers or hosts is the page's audience)

section_sequence.section: Hero (what the supply side gets + join)
section_sequence.purpose: What joining gives the supply side (the orders, customers or bookings it reaches) in one headline, and the supply side's own action: apply, list, or join. A real screen of the supplier's view beside it. The buyer path is a text link at most.
The reach, the orders and the tools the supply side gets, each with its concrete result.
Three to five steps from joining to getting paid: apply, list, receive orders, deliver, get paid. Real supplier screens where the client has them.
The supplier tools (orders, catalog, payouts, reports), one row each with a real screen.
Fees, payout timing, coverage and the requirements to join, stated plainly. This answers what a supplier asks before applying.
Real numbers the supply side cares about (buyers reached, orders a month, cities), measured by the client.
One named quote from a real supplier, with the business name and city.

What it costs to join, how long onboarding takes, when payouts land, what happens with returns. Its questions come from the brief's objections, each in the customer's own words turned into a question; with no objections in the brief, it answers only the operational questions the client's own material answers.
Repeats the supply side's action with the same verb, one filled button.
Sitemap footer: For suppliers, For buyers, Company, Legal.

entries.cta_placement: The supply side's action (apply, list or join) in the hero and the closing band; the buyer path as a text link in the header.
entries.footer: Sitemap footer: For suppliers, For buyers, Company, Legal.
entries.notes: The page speaks to the supply side, so the buyer-only sections (categories to shop, how ordering works, delivery to the buyer) are left out. Icons follow the one icon rule in commands/ux-design.md: one set per page, an icon only where it says something distinct about its item.
